passage: In urban planning, city officials often try to relieve traffic congestion by widening highways or constructing additional lanes. Paradoxically, transportation researchers have consistently observed that expanding road capacity rarely reduces gridlock over the long term—a phenomenon known as induced demand. When a congested route becomes faster, commuters who previously took public transit, traveled during off-peak hours, or avoided unnecessary trips quickly switch back to driving on the newly widened road. Within a few years, vehicle volume rises to match the expanded capacity, returning travel times to their previous sluggish levels while increasing carbon emissions and maintenance costs. Lasting relief from congestion therefore depends less on pouring more asphalt and more on investing in reliable mass transit, dedicated bus lanes, and walkable neighborhood design.
